title: The cowherd's skills
hookLine: eleven skills of a good cowherd, and of a good monk

lines: ASK A FARMER: NOT LOVE, BUT FLIES.
ELEVEN OF THEM, ONE BY ONE.
cards: Ask an old herder what the job is, and the answer may have little to do with love of animals or a sense of calling. It may be about flies. Wounds.
Which field still has grass in August. Whether you know your own cows by sight. Herding is a craft of small, boring, crucial skills.
The Buddha once listed eleven of them, one by one, and then showed that each was also a skill of the spiritual life.

teach.h: ELEVEN SKILLS OF A GOOD COWHERD
teach.b: This is the greater discourse on the cowherd, the thirty-third of the Middle-Length Sayings. A good cowherd knows the shape of his cattle and their markings.
He picks the flies' eggs out of their hides and dresses their wounds. He makes smoke to drive the insects off. He knows the watering place, and knows when they've had enough to drink.
He knows the road, and good pasture. He doesn't milk them dry, but leaves some for the calves. And he gives special honor to the bulls who father and lead the herd.
Now the Buddha turns each one. Knowing the shape of the cattle is knowing the body: what it's made of. Knowing the markings is knowing that a fool and a wise person are marked by what they do.

Picking out the flies' eggs is not letting thoughts of sensual desire, ill will and cruelty settle in and hatch. Dressing the wounds is guarding the senses. Making smoke is teaching others what you've learned.
The watering place is going to people who know more, and asking questions. Knowing when they've drunk is feeling the meaning land. The road is the eightfold path.
The pasture is the four foundations of mindfulness.

teach.h: A CRAFT, LEARNED SKILL BY SKILL
teach.b: Not milking dry is accepting only what you need from people who give.
And honoring the lead bulls is kindness toward the elder monks, in deed, word and thought, openly and in private. Not one is a vision or a miracle. Flies' eggs.
Smoke. The spiritual life, here, is a craft, learned one small skill at a time.

how: Buddhist teachers often draw on farming and herding similes like MN 33 to present practice as a set of learnable skills: restraint of the senses, removing harmful thoughts, asking those more learned, moderation in what one accepts, and respect for elders.

o: a guard who keeps watch at a city gate
a farmer who owns many fields of grain
a cowherd, skilled at tending the herd

games.q: the cowherd and the monk — tap the pairs.

s: a good cowherd takes every drop of milk
he doesn't milk dry; he leaves some, as a monk accepts only what he needs from those who give.
the road, in the simile, is the eightfold path
and the pasture is the four foundations of mindfulness.
most of the eleven skills are about visions and miracles
they're plain crafts: flies' eggs, smoke, wounds, water and pasture.

games.q: you're a cowherd. you spot flies' eggs on a cow's hide. it's late, and you're tired. what does a good cowherd do?
o: pick them out now, before they hatch.
games.why: a good cowherd picks the eggs out. the Buddha's monk does the same with thoughts of sensual desire, ill will and cruelty, before they settle in.

practice: Watch the mind, and when a sour thought lands, irritation, envy, a little cruelty, don't fight it and don't feed it.
Notice it the way a cowherd spots an egg on a hide, and gently brush it off by coming back to the breath, as often as the next one lands.

wordCard.voice: gopalaka. Eleven plain crafts of tending a herd, each one a craft of tending a mind.

orig.note: Pali gopalaka: cowherd (go, cow + palaka, keeper). the discourse is the Mahagopalaka Sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: know your herd. Flies' eggs and smoke count as practice too. Day four hundred twenty-nine, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 33, Mahagopalaka Sutta (the greater discourse on the cowherd)
